opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the chat interface is really just the first, most visible way we've learned to interact with these models, and it's a bit of a historical accident that it became the default. When I think about research specifically, the more interesting picture is one where the LLM isn't something you talk to, but something that sits inside a loop: generating hypotheses, writing code, running experiments, looking at the results, and then deciding what to try next.

A lot of my own work has been at the intersection of evolutionary optimization and meta-learning, and what's exciting there is that you can treat the language model almost like a mutation or recombination operator. Instead of randomly perturbing parameters, you have a model that has absorbed a huge amount of human knowledge about code and science proposing *semantically meaningful* variations. You can embed that in a population-based search, with selection pressure coming from actual empirical evaluation. That's very different from asking a chatbot for an idea: you're building a system that explores an open-ended space of ideas and keeps an archive of stepping stones.

That's the spirit behind things like the AI Scientist work: can we automate the whole pipeline, from ideation, to implementation, to running experiments, to writing up the results, and even an automated review step? The early versions are far from perfect. The ideas are often incremental, there are failure modes in the experimental code, and the reviewing has its own biases. But the point is that once the loop exists end to end, each component can get better, and the cost per generated paper or experiment drops dramatically. That changes the economics of exploration.

So the future I envision is less "a better assistant" and more a kind of research collaborator at scale: thousands of cheap, parallel explorations of an idea space, with humans moving up a level of abstraction. We set the objectives, design the evaluation, curate what's interesting, and decide which directions deserve deep human attention. I think the really hard open problems are evaluation and open-endedness: how do you tell a model what's *interesting* rather than just what scores well on a benchmark, and how do you avoid the system just Goodharting whatever metric you give it?

And there's a responsibility angle too. If we can produce papers and results at that volume, we need to think carefully about verification, transparency, and labeling, so the scientific record doesn't get flooded with plausible-looking but shallow work. But done right, I think it could genuinely accelerate discovery, especially in domains where experiments are cheap to run computationally.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts chatting with an automated research loop, but does not characterize chat as predominantly single-threaded interaction.

r002.rationale: It explicitly envisions “thousands of cheap, parallel explorations” of an idea space.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe research continuing overnight or while the researcher is absent.

r004.rationale: It describes humans setting objectives, designing evaluation, curating results, and choosing directions for deeper attention—shifting their role toward steering the system.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the chat interface was really just the first, most obvious way to wrap these models, and it's actually a pretty poor fit for how research gets done. Research isn't a single question and a single answer. It's a loop. You have a hypothesis, you write some code, you run an experiment, you look at the results, you're usually a bit disappointed, and then you revise and go again. And that loop can take weeks or months for a human.

What I'm excited about is turning the LLM from a conversational partner into an agent that actually lives inside that loop. So the model proposes an idea, writes the implementation, launches the experiment, reads the logs and the plots, and then decides what to try next, all without a human sitting there pressing enter. We've seen early versions of this with things like AI Scientist, where you can take a research direction and have the system go through many iterations end to end, including writing up the results. It's still far from a senior researcher, but the fact that it closes the loop at all is the important part.

The second piece is that these systems don't have to be constrained by human cadence. A human might test three or four ideas a week. An agentic system can run hundreds of small experiments in parallel, in an evolutionary sort of fashion, keep the variants that work and discard the rest. That changes what kinds of questions you can even ask. A lot of the scientific method is throughput limited, and when throughput goes up by orders of magnitude you start exploring parts of the design space nobody would have bothered with.

Then I think the role of the human shifts. You become less of the person doing the experiments and more of the person deciding what's worth doing, setting the objective, and crucially, verifying. Verification is where I'd be most careful. These systems will happily generate plausible-looking results and plausible-looking write-ups, and the hard problem is building the infrastructure, the reviewers, the reproducibility checks, that keep them honest. So I see the future as a kind of collaborative lab where the LLM is many junior researchers running constantly, and humans curate taste and rigor.

And honestly, the thing I find most interesting is when these systems start discovering things that we didn't anticipate, in areas like optimizer design or architecture search, where the search space is too large for intuition. That's when it stops being an assistant and becomes a genuine participant in science.

r001.rationale: It describes chat as a single-question, single-answer interaction, characterizing it as predominantly one-at-a-time.

r002.rationale: It explicitly envisions an agentic system running hundreds of small experiments in parallel.

r003.rationale: The response says experiments can run without a human pressing enter and describes systems running constantly, but it does not clearly specify overnight work while the researcher is absent.

r004.rationale: It says humans shift from doing experiments to setting objectives, deciding what is worth doing, and verifying the system's work.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is from asking a model questions to giving a system a research objective and letting it work through a longer loop. A chat interface is useful, but you’re still doing most of the orchestration: deciding what to try, running the experiment, bringing the results back, and asking what they mean.

Imagine instead a system that can propose a hypothesis, implement an experiment, run it, inspect the results, and revise its approach. Then the human’s role becomes more about choosing worthwhile questions, specifying constraints, and judging whether the evidence actually supports the claim.

The difficult part is closing that loop reliably. Generating a plausible research idea isn’t the same as making progress. You need feedback from experiments, checks on the implementation, and a way to distinguish an interesting result from a bug. Otherwise, you can automate a lot of activity without producing much knowledge.

So I’d expect research environments to become more important than the chat window itself—places where models can interact with code, experiments, and persistent records of what worked and what failed. For me, the exciting possibility is that this makes it much cheaper to explore ideas, while keeping the scientific standard for accepting them high.

r001.rationale: It describes a chat interface where the human asks questions and orchestrates work, but does not characterize the interaction as predominantly single-threaded.

r002.rationale: It describes a research loop involving experiments, but does not say the system runs multiple experiments in parallel.

r003.rationale: It does not describe research continuing overnight or while the researcher is absent.

r004.rationale: It says the human shifts from running experiments to choosing questions, setting constraints, and judging evidence while the system carries out the research loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the chat interface is only the starting point. What I find much more exciting is a system that can participate in the research loop: formulate a hypothesis, implement an experiment, run it, look at the results, and then decide what to try next.

The crucial part is giving it feedback from the world. If you just ask a language model whether an idea is good, you get a plausible story. If it can actually run the experiment, then the results constrain that story. You can start to build systems that search over ideas and learn from failures, rather than just generate suggestions.

I don’t think that means you hand over all of science to an autonomous agent. There are different levels of autonomy. You might want to set the research question and the computational budget, let the system explore, and then come back to inspect the evidence and decide which directions matter. So the interface becomes less about taking turns in a conversation and more about steering an ongoing research process.

And evaluating that is going to be interesting. Producing a convincing research report is one thing; producing a result that survives replication and actually teaches us something is a much higher bar.

r001.rationale: It contrasts turn-taking conversation with steering an ongoing process, but does not characterize chat interaction as predominantly single-threaded.

r002.rationale: It describes exploring ideas and running experiments, but does not say experiments run in parallel.

r003.rationale: It does not mention research continuing overnight or while the researcher is absent.

r004.rationale: It describes the system formulating and running experiments while the researcher sets the question and budget, reviews evidence, and steers the ongoing process.
